paper.title_en: The Role of Scintillation in Detecting HI Absorption in FRB Spectra
paper.abstract_en: The 21 cm absorption line of neutral hydrogen has been a long hypothesized observational feature of fast radio burst (FRB) spectra. Difficulties associated with detector noise in extracting HI absorption have been previously studied. We test the role that scintillation plays in its detectability and characterize the regimes where a realistic FRB may yield the 21 cm line. We build an efficient model to simulate diffractive scintillation arising from FRB passage through a thin scattering screen. We find that the absorption profile is detectable in a scintillation-dominated high signal-to-noise spectrum if the scintillation decorrelation bandwidth differs significantly in scale from absorption profile width. Specifically, for a detector with a known SEFD, the HI line can be extracted using a low-pass filter for scintillation bandwidths $< 0.5$ kHz, peak cloud optical depths $> 0.5$, and fluences $\gtrsim$ SEFD Jy ms (assuming a 1 ms duration). Stacking repeat bursts from active repeaters is also useful, but they must be separated in time by more than the diffractive scintillation timescale, otherwise flux modulations with frequency are correlated. By cross-referencing repeating FRB positions with a catalog of Milky Way molecular clouds detected in CO, we find that the sightline to FRB 20180916B may intersect a Galactic molecular cloud. This possibility may be confirmed with a hundred or more baseband-recorded bursts with GBT. We also identify clear observation strategies with FAST and GBT for a range of repeater luminosity functions, with both telescopes needing roughly 500 bursts to confidently detect a peak optical depth of $0.5$.
